content_html:
SpiNNaker — Reading System State & Interpreting Outputs

SpiNNaker’s “outputs” are neural signals. You read them as spikes and state variables, then decode their meaning statistically or use them directly to actuate devices. It’s closer to neuroscience recording than to reading a CPU register.

In SpiNNaker, there is no single global state or scalar “answer.” State is the evolving distribution of spikes, membrane variables, and synaptic parameters across millions of lightweight neuron processes. You read it by recording spike trains, voltages, and plasticity variables via PyNN/sPyNNaker, either online (streaming) or offline (post-run). Outputs are spatiotemporal patterns of activity that you decode statistically or use directly to drive robots/devices.

1) What “State” Means on SpiNNaker

  • Local neuron state: membrane voltage v, synaptic conductances g, input currents I, thresholds, refractory timers.
  • Synapse state: weights, delays, plasticity variables (e.g., STDP traces).
  • Network structure: routing tables (the effective connectivity graph), partition mappings.
  • Activity history: spike times per neuron (emitted spikes) and optionally received spikes.

2) How You Read It (Host ↔ SpiNNaker I/O)

  1. Define the model in PyNN (or sPyNNaker).
  2. Deploy to SpiNNaker; network partitions onto many cores.
  3. Choose recording modes (spikes/voltages/weights) for selected populations.
  4. Run in real time; data are streamed to the host or buffered for post-run retrieval.
  5. Analyze on the host (NumPy, pandas, plots); save to HDF5/CSV.

3) Outputs You Can Record

Output Type What It Looks Like What It Tells You
Spike trains
(raster)		 List of (neuron id, time) events Timing codes, firing rates, synchronization, patterns (assemblies)
Membrane traces Time series of
v(t)
,
g(t)
,
I(t)		 Oscillations, bursting, adaptation, resonance
Synaptic variables Weights/delays, STDP traces over time Learning, consolidation, connectivity changes
Population summaries Firing-rate histograms, mean voltage, weight distributions Mesoscale dynamics, stability, phase transitions
Routing/connectivity Routing tables, adjacency matrices Effective network structure and mapping quality
Real-time spike streams Outbound packets to devices/robots Direct control signals (e.g., motor rates, decisions)

4) Online vs Offline Readout

Mode How Use Case
Online (streaming) Spikes/variables sent as they occur Closed-loop robotics, interactive experiments, BCIs
Offline (post-run) Buffers flushed after execution Large neuroscience models; heavy analysis without I/O bottlenecks
Hybrid Partial streaming + partial buffering Monitoring while preserving throughput

5) Decoding “Meaning” from Outputs

  • Perception: orientation maps, receptive fields from V1-like models.
  • Decision: winner–take–all firing rates; choice decoded from population activity.
  • Memory: sequence replay; similarity of spike patterns across time.
  • Motor control: spike counts → PWM/velocity for actuators.

Typical analyses: raster plots, peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTH), autocorrelograms, coherence/power spectra, dimensionality reduction (PCA/t-SNE/UMAP), functional connectivity graphs.

6) Minimal PyNN Readout Pattern (Concept)

# Conceptual sketch (backend could be pyNN.spiNNaker)
pop.record(['spikes', 'v'])      # choose outputs
sim.run(1000)                    # run 1000 ms
data = pop.get_data(['spikes','v'])
# analyze: spikes.as_array(), v.as_array() → plots, stats, decoding

7) Practical Notes

  • Sampling costs: Recording too many variables can reduce real-time performance—sample selectively.
  • Clocklessness: Without a global clock, align events by timestamps; use host time or simulation timesteps.
  • Scalability: Prefer population summaries for very large models; downsample neuron traces.
  • Validation: Cross-check routing/connectivity dumps against intended topology.
